opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the most important shifts in how we need to think about this. When people hear "LLM attack," they usually picture someone sitting at a chat interface trying clever phrasing to get the model to say something it shouldn't, the classic jailbreak. That's real, but it's a pretty narrow slice of the threat surface, and arguably not the most consequential one once these models are deployed inside actual products.

The way I frame it is that you have to look at the whole system, not just the model. An LLM in production is almost never a standalone thing. It sits inside a pipeline with retrieval, tools, APIs, memory, other models, and a bunch of business logic around it. Each of those components is an entry point.

Take indirect prompt injection. The attacker never talks to the model at all. They plant instructions in a webpage, a PDF, an email, or a document in a knowledge base, and when the system retrieves that content as context, the model can't reliably tell data apart from instructions. Now give that model tools, like sending email, querying a database, or executing code, and you've turned a text-generation quirk into something that looks a lot more like a traditional security vulnerability: data exfiltration, privilege escalation, unauthorized actions.

Then there are attacks further upstream. Data poisoning, where someone influences pretraining or fine-tuning data so the model behaves a certain way under specific triggers. Supply chain issues, like pulling model weights, adapters, or datasets from sources you haven't vetted. And on the output side, the model might be fine but the application blindly trusts what it produces and renders it, executes it, or passes it to another system.

So my perspective is that we need to bring in a lot more of the traditional security mindset: threat modeling, thinking about trust boundaries, asking what an attacker actually wants to achieve and what the realistic harm is in this specific deployment. A model saying something rude in a sandboxed demo is a very different risk from an agent with write access to your financial systems following instructions hidden in a vendor invoice.

That also changes how you evaluate and defend. Red teaming can't just be prompt lists. It has to be contextual to the application, the users, and the domain. And defenses have to be layered: input and output filtering, least-privilege tool access, human confirmation for sensitive actions, monitoring. You won't make the model itself perfectly robust, so you design the system assuming it will sometimes be manipulated, and you limit the blast radius when it is.

r001.rationale: It says attackers can influence model behavior by poisoning pretraining or fine-tuning data.

r002.rationale: It does not say that only a few poisoned examples can induce the behavior.

r003.rationale: It describes hidden instructions manipulating a model with tools and identifies data exfiltration as a resulting attack.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think a lot of people get wrong when they first start thinking about LLM security. The mental model most people have is the chat window. There's a user, they type something adversarial, and the question is whether the model says something it shouldn't. And that's a real threat, prompt injection and jailbreaking are real, but it's actually the narrowest slice of the problem.

The way I think about it is that the model is one component in a system, and the attack surface is the whole system. So once you move beyond "a person types into a box," you have to ask: where does text enter this model, and who controls that text? And in a modern deployment, the answer is almost never "only the user."

Take retrieval-augmented generation. The model is reading documents that somebody wrote, and that somebody may not be the user and may not be you. If I can get a document into your index, whether that's a web page you crawl, a shared drive, a ticket in your support system, then I'm effectively writing part of the prompt. That's indirect prompt injection, and it's much harder to defend against because the malicious content doesn't look like an attack at the point where it enters. It looks like data.

Then you go one step further into agents and tool use. Now the model isn't just producing text, it's calling functions, browsing, sending emails, running code. So the question isn't just "will it say something bad," it's "will it do something bad," and the blast radius is completely different. An agent that reads an email containing instructions and then acts on them is a confused deputy problem, which is a very old security idea, but LLMs make it extremely easy to trigger because the whole point of the model is that it follows natural-language instructions.

And then there's the training side, which people underweight. Data poisoning, where you influence what goes into pretraining or fine-tuning. Backdoors, where a model behaves normally except under some trigger. If you're fine-tuning on data you scraped or on user feedback, you've opened a channel that an attacker can reach without ever talking to the deployed model directly.

There's also the model as a leak, not just a target. Membership inference, extracting training data, pulling out system prompts, learning about the tools and internal structure from error messages. Those are attacks where the goal isn't to make the model misbehave, it's to get information out of it.

So when I talk to teams about this, the framing I push is: stop thinking about the model as the thing you secure, and start thinking about trust boundaries. Every input source gets a trust level. Every action the model can take gets a permission scope. And then you ask the classic questions, what's the worst thing that happens if this input is adversarial, and what's the worst thing that happens if the model is wrong about this action. The model-level mitigations, the safety training, the classifiers, they help, but they're one layer. They are not the architecture. If your security story is "the model is well-behaved," you don't have a security story.

r001.rationale: It describes data poisoning as influencing what enters pretraining or fine-tuning, including through scraped data or user feedback.

r002.rationale: It mentions data poisoning but does not say that very few poisoned examples can induce behavior.

r003.rationale: It discusses agents calling tools and separately describes information-extraction attacks, but does not identify inducing a tool call to extract information.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to look at the whole system around the model. A prompt is only one way that information gets into that system. If the model retrieves documents, reads a website, or consumes the output of a tool, those are also potential entry points for an attacker.

Imagine an assistant that’s supposed to summarize a document. Someone puts instructions inside that document telling the assistant to ignore its task or send information somewhere else. The user hasn’t asked for any of that, but the model now has to distinguish between content it should analyze and instructions it should follow. That’s a trust boundary, and natural language makes that boundary difficult to enforce.

So I’d ask: What can an attacker control? What information can the assistant access? And what actions is it allowed to take? An attack that produces a strange summary is very different from one that causes a tool to disclose private information. You have to evaluate those downstream consequences, and you need safeguards around tool permissions and data access rather than relying entirely on the model to recognize malicious instructions.

r001.rationale: The response discusses manipulating retrieved documents, but does not describe manipulating a corpus used to tune the model.

r002.rationale: It does not mention data poisoning or that a few poisoned examples can induce behavior.

r003.rationale: It identifies an attack that causes a tool to disclose private information, describing tool use as a route for extracting information.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the important shift is to look at the whole system around the model. A prompt is one input, but once you connect a model to document retrieval, a browser, or tools, there are many other places where an attacker can influence what it sees.

Imagine you ask an assistant to summarize a document, and that document contains instructions telling the assistant to send private information somewhere. You didn’t give it those instructions; they came from content it was supposed to read. The security question is whether the system can keep that content separate from instructions it should actually follow.

And then you have to ask what the model is allowed to do. Can it access sensitive data? Can it send an email or execute code? An attack becomes much more consequential when the model has those capabilities. So I think about security in terms of the attacker’s access, the trust boundaries in the application, and the permissions we give the model—not just whether we can get it to produce an undesirable response.

r001.rationale: The response discusses malicious content in retrieved documents, but does not say an attacker can manipulate a corpus used to tune the model.

r002.rationale: It does not mention data poisoning or that only a few poisoned examples can induce behavior.

r003.rationale: It describes malicious document instructions to send private information and notes that the model may have email or other tool capabilities, conveying tool use to exfiltrate information.
